title: Prospective transport of causal policy effects across populations

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a dependable way to predict what an economic policy will cause in a specified new population before the policy’s effects are observed there. It would combine evidence from earlier experiments with information about the target population, state which causal relationships are assumed to remain stable, and produce an effect prediction with informative uncertainty and explicit applicability limits. The ambition is prospectively validated policy transport: predictions that survive subsequent target trials, rather than adjustments that look successful after both settings’ outcomes are already known.

Transportability theory already supplies identification criteria and formulas conditional on a causal model and available data. A selection diagram represents assumptions about which mechanisms differ between populations; those assumptions determine whether source experiments and target observations can identify the target effect. The proposed breakthrough therefore goes beyond deriving another transport formula. It requires making the assumptions operational enough, and validating their consequences reliably enough, to support decisions in specified economic-policy settings.

Three kinds of transfer need to be distinguished. Population composition can change the average effect even when a policy works through stable mechanisms. A different implementer can change the treatment actually delivered. Expansion to a different scale may change the environment in which the policy operates. As a proposed scope rule, population transport is central to this entry, while implementation and scale changes require additional, separately tested assumptions. Success on one kind of transfer would not establish success on the others.

significance.text: Randomized trials and credible quasi-experiments can identify causal effects within their designs and assumptions, while policy decisions concern populations and delivery conditions beyond those studies. Reliable transport would make earlier experiments reusable for those decisions without assuming that the next setting is identical. The direct advance would be better-grounded estimates of target effects, accompanied by an account of which differences between settings matter and which measurements are needed to bridge them.

Conditional consequence: informative prospective predictions could help governments compare programs, decide where local experimentation is essential, and concentrate data collection on consequential differences. They might reduce unnecessary repetition of experiments and make evidence useful earlier in a policy decision. These benefits depend on predictive accuracy, useful uncertainty, measurement costs and the decisions actually made; successful statistical calibration alone would not establish improved policy outcomes or welfare.

Portability beyond a medicine’s first trial is an illustrative analogy for the ambition. It does not imply that economic policies would transfer universally, or that medical evidence itself transfers without qualification. Likewise, a system that can issue useful warnings about questionable transport would add value, but accurate effect intervals do not by themselves demonstrate reliable detection of invalid assumptions. In the supplied advertising manuscript’s setup, a central transport assumption involves counterfactual quantities and cannot be checked directly from the observed data.

missing_breakthrough.text: The unsolved capability proposed here is informative, prospectively validated transport across specified economic-policy populations and implementation settings, with explicit limits on applicability. Existing mathematical results do not supply the necessary causal knowledge automatically. Investigators must determine which mechanisms remain invariant, how population differences arise, and whether the available experimental and observational measurements identify the desired target effect. The supplied evidence documents these requirements and practical difficulties, but does not establish how frequently they prevent transport or prove that no qualifying capability existed by November 1, 2026.

Unmeasured effect modifiers are a concrete obstacle: source and target populations may differ along dimensions that change policy response but were unavailable when predictions were made. Implementation differences create another problem because an apparently shared program label may conceal different interventions. Vivalt’s reported heterogeneity, including smaller effects for government-implemented programs after controlling for sample size, motivates testing across delivery arrangements. That association does not establish that implementer identity itself causes the difference, nor that measuring implementer identity would resolve it.

Uncertainty about the transport assumptions must also be separated from ordinary sampling uncertainty. A precise source estimate need not yield a reliable target prediction when the assumed relationship between settings is wrong. The advertising preprint illustrates sensitivity analysis for departures from transportability, while explicitly acknowledging that its sensitivity parameter is not identifiable. Such calculations can expose dependence on assumptions; they do not establish which departure actually holds or provide a universal empirical detector of transport failure.

Engineering synthesis: an operational method would need to specify comparable treatments and outcomes, document what target information was available at prediction time, handle settings poorly represented by the source evidence, and produce reproducible predictions before target outcomes are revealed. It would also need to distinguish a changed population from a changed intervention or policy environment. These are proposed requirements for the capability, rather than evidence that one particular method has already satisfied them.

current_state.text: The supplied review identifies a retained Pearl–Bareinboim technical report, Transportability across studies: A formal approach, first issued in 2011 and revised in August 2018. It develops selection diagrams and do-calculus criteria for transport under specified causal assumptions. Its discussion distinguishes these criteria from a recursive theorem that the report itself describes as incomplete. This document establishes substantive mathematical foundations, but it is a different document from the 2014 Statistical Science article named in the earlier research. No retained copy of that article was available in the supplied evidence, so its exact contents cannot be verified through the report.

The scoping review by Manke-Reimers and colleagues, published April 18, 2025, searched publications from 2010 through December 18, 2024. It included 64 numerical transportability studies: 44 methodological studies and 20 pure applications. Seventeen of the 20 pure applications transported randomized-trial effects. The reviewed examples were predominantly health-related, with housing and other policy applications also represented. These counts describe the review’s inclusion scope, which excluded grey literature and fully overlapping generalizability applications; they are not a census of all methods for transferring policy evidence. The review did not assess study quality.

A particularly relevant finding was that, among reviewed studies lacking complete target-population data, none compared the transported estimate with a target-population effect estimate. This supports the importance of direct target validation, but does not establish the absence of prospective economic-policy validation elsewhere. The supplied review retained the scoping article’s main text; its figures and supplementary files were not inspected.

Vivalt’s 2020 article reports substantial heterogeneity across development impact evaluations and smaller effect sizes for government-implemented programs than for academic or nongovernmental implementations, even after controlling for sample size. The supplied evidence supports this through the IDEAS abstract record. Full-text access was restricted, and neither the complete analysis nor an independent JSTOR confirmation was supplied. The result motivates attention to implementation, but does not isolate a causal effect of implementer type or establish the prevalence of hidden effect modifiers.

Pritchett’s May 2021 working paper offers a qualified education example involving private versus public schooling. Its abstract reports that, under plausible assumptions, exclusive reliance on rigorous external evidence produces root mean squared error three times worse than using each context’s biased ordinary-least-squares estimate. This quantitative comparison is supported at the abstract level in the supplied material. It is an example of the possible cost of poor external prediction, not a general finding that local observational estimates outperform transported experimental evidence.

The Miao, Zhao and Kang preprint was submitted November 2, 2024, with the reviewed version dated June 23, 2026. Its political-advertising application shows that small assumed departures from transportability can change county-level conclusions about turnout effects, including whether effects appear positive, negative or statistically distinguishable from zero. These are conditional sensitivity calculations, not observed target-trial reversals. A material qualification is that the manuscript reports no county remaining sensitive after its Bonferroni correction. The relevant main-text sections were retained, but extraction ended during page 72 of a longer supplement; the supplementary correction results were beyond the retained extraction, and figures were not visually inspected.

Taken together, the supplied sources establish transportability theory, numerical applications, empirical heterogeneity and methods for examining sensitivity to transport assumptions. They do not establish that the proposed prospective capability has been achieved, nor do they establish its field-wide absence as of November 1, 2026. The systematic review’s search ends in December 2024, and the June 2026 preprint does not provide a comprehensive later survey. This limitation leaves the frontier unresolved without negating the documented results.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: pre-register and publish target-effect predictions, uncertainty intervals and applicability rules before observing target-trial outcomes. Specify the source evidence, target population, treatment, outcome, prediction horizon, available target information and evaluation rules in advance. Target covariates or other permitted observations may inform the prediction, but target outcomes used for validation must remain unavailable until predictions are fixed. Reweighting fitted after inspecting both outcome datasets would not meet this prospective requirement.
completion_criteria.label: Target-effect predictions are preregistered and published before target outcomes

completion_criteria.text: Proposed validation suite: include meaningfully different target populations, government and researcher implementations, and separately identified changes in scale. Include stress tests in which a modifier unavailable at prediction time is subsequently measured and shown to matter. Specify the suite and its size in advance, with enough independent target settings to evaluate predictive reliability. Report performance separately for population differences, implementation changes and scale changes so that success in one category does not stand in for another.
completion_criteria.label: Prespecified target validation separately tests population, implementation and scale changes

completion_criteria.text: Proposed success assessment: evaluate calibration while accounting for sampling uncertainty in target experimental estimates. Coverage of noisy estimates differs from coverage of the underlying causal effects, and broad intervals can obtain high coverage while offering little decision value. Require informative interval widths and predictive performance against pre-specified baselines, with explicit rules for evaluating bias, error and uncertainty. The supplied evidence does not determine a numerical pass threshold; any thresholds would need to be justified for the intended policy decisions.
completion_criteria.label: Informative intervals demonstrate calibration accounting for target sampling uncertainty

completion_criteria.text: Proposed applicability assessment: score warnings and abstentions separately from effect predictions. Report how often the method makes a prediction, how informative those predictions are, and whether its warnings discriminate settings where errors become consequential. A method should not receive credit for detecting invalid transport merely because its intervals are calibrated, nor for broad usefulness if it declines nearly every difficult case. Claims about warnings must remain bounded by the assumptions and information available to the method.
completion_criteria.label: Warnings and abstentions are scored separately from effect predictions

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: release sufficient protocols, data or permissible verification materials, code and prediction records for independent teams to reproduce the results and repeat the exercise on new targets. Document measurement and implementation costs and the settings in which the method remains useful. A finite trial suite could establish demonstrated breadth across its tested conditions; it could not establish literal universality, transfer to arbitrary interventions, or reliable prediction under wholly new macroeconomic regimes. These are proposed demonstrations, not established completion standards.
completion_criteria.label: Independent teams reproduce results and repeat predictions on new targets

related_concepts.text: Roster-based scope synthesis: ECO-08, Structural counterfactuals for macroeconomic regimes, is the closest boundary. ECO-02 asks whether effects learned elsewhere can be transported under explicit assumptions about stable mechanisms; ECO-08 concerns counterfactuals under changes to the macroeconomic rules agents face. Population composition, implementation and scale can sometimes interact with those rules, so the boundary must be specified for each application. Assigning wholly new macroeconomic regimes to ECO-08 preserves the proposed editorial distinction. Only ECO-08’s title was supplied, so a more detailed comparison remains provisional.

Roster-based scope synthesis: ECO-01, Empirically valid aggregate market laws beyond the Sonnenschein–Mantel–Debreu barrier, and ECO-07, A verified, manipulable law of sustained productivity growth, seek regularities that could help explain or predict economic responses. Such regularities could inform assumptions used in transport. ECO-02 instead concerns whether particular causal policy effects travel between specified settings; successful transport would not by itself establish aggregate market laws or a manipulable law of productivity growth.

Roster-based scope synthesis: ECO-03, A predictive and welfare-coherent theory of boundedly rational choice, could help explain behavioral differences that affect policy response. ECO-04, An interpersonally comparable, preference-respecting measure of welfare, concerns how outcomes should be evaluated across people. ECO-02 addresses prediction of causal effects. Accurate transport of an outcome does not establish a theory of choice, interpersonal welfare comparability or whether the resulting policy is desirable.

Roster-based scope synthesis: ECO-05, Approximately efficient voluntary provision of global public goods, and ECO-09, A general, detail-free allocation compiler for private-information economies, concern provision and allocation mechanisms. Transport methods could help evaluate how a particular mechanism performs across populations, while mechanism design could clarify which intervention is being transported. Predicting those effects would not establish approximate efficiency, incentive properties or a general allocation compiler.

Roster-based scope synthesis: ECO-06, Household-scale markets for national, occupational, and housing income risk, and ECO-10, Liquidity and credit without run-prone debt, concern financial arrangements whose effects might require evaluation across populations and institutions. ECO-02 could support assessment of particular implementations. It does not itself create those markets or demonstrate the elimination of run-prone debt. These entries remain distinct innovations.

The mathematical foundations of ECO-02 overlap substantially with statistics, epidemiology and computer science. The economics-specific contribution proposed here is the prospective validation of policy-effect predictions under economically meaningful population and delivery differences. Existing cross-disciplinary transportability methods are foundations and potential components of that capability.

change_log.change: Reframed the missing breakthrough as prospectively validated policy transport with informative uncertainty and explicit applicability limits.
change_log.reason: Transport formulas already exist; the proposed advance concerns their operational reliability and validation in specified policy settings.

change_log.change: Separated population composition, implementation changes and scale changes throughout the record.
change_log.reason: These differences can affect distinct causal mechanisms, and evidence for one kind of transfer does not validate the others.

change_log.change: Corrected the foundational source attribution to the retained technical report first issued in 2011 and revised in August 2018, using its supplied resolved URL.
change_log.reason: The report was bundled under the scoping-review source record but is a separate document. It cannot verify the exact contents of the uncaptured 2014 article.

change_log.change: Preserved the scoping review’s 64-study total, 44 methodological studies, 20 pure applications and 17 randomized-trial applications, while adding its search dates and exclusions.
change_log.reason: The quantitative findings are supported within the review’s scope and should not be generalized into a census or proof of current field-wide absence.

change_log.change: Integrated the review’s finding about missing target-effect comparisons and preserved its inspection limitations.
change_log.reason: The finding motivates prospective target validation, while uninspected figures and supplements limit what can be inferred from the supplied review.

change_log.change: Retained Vivalt’s implementation association and removed claims of session reconfirmation or JSTOR verification.
change_log.reason: The supplied IDEAS abstract supports the association; full analysis and independent JSTOR confirmation were not supplied, and the association is not causal identification of implementer effects.

change_log.change: Preserved Pritchett’s threefold RMSE comparison with its education setting, assumptions and abstract-level access.
change_log.reason: The numerical detail is supported as a qualified example, not as a general ranking of local observational and transported experimental estimates.

change_log.change: Recast the advertising result as preprint sensitivity analysis and included the Bonferroni qualification and extraction limits.
change_log.reason: Assumed departures can change conclusions without demonstrating observed target-effect reversals; the reported multiplicity correction materially limits the county-level interpretation.

change_log.change: Strengthened the proposed completion demonstration with target-estimate uncertainty, informative interval widths, baselines, independent replication and separate warning evaluation.
change_log.reason: Nominal coverage alone can be uninformative and does not establish reliable detection of invalid transport.

change_log.change: Qualified the medicine analogy and downstream benefits, and removed the unsupported assertion that current transfer decisions are mostly judgment.
change_log.reason: The analogy illustrates the ambition, while improved outcomes, universal portability and reliable failure detection require additional evidence.

change_log.change: Explained relationships to every other supplied roster entry while marking title-based comparisons as scope synthesis.
change_log.reason: The roster supplies titles rather than full concept records, so detailed overlaps cannot be treated as verified descriptions.

unresolved_issues: The supplied evidence does not establish whether a system satisfying the proposed prospective criteria existed as of November 1, 2026. Its absence should not be inferred from the dated sources.
The cited 2014 Statistical Science article has no retained artifact. Its exact relationship to the reviewed 2018 technical report remains unverified in the supplied material.
The prevalence and practical importance of unmeasured effect modifiers, treatment changes and incorrect causal diagrams across economic-policy transport applications are not quantified here.
Vivalt’s full analysis and Pritchett’s full working paper were not supplied for review; their retained findings are supported at the abstract level.

The advertising manuscript’s supplementary correction results extend beyond the retained extraction. The main text reports no sensitive county after Bonferroni correction, but the underlying supplementary details were not available in the supplied review.
The number and diversity of target trials, useful interval widths, comparison baselines and decision-relevant success thresholds remain to be specified for any actual demonstration.
Reliable applicability warnings remain a separate open capability: the supplied sensitivity analysis does not establish general detection of false transport assumptions.
Only roster titles were supplied for the related concepts. The proposed boundary with ECO-08 and other overlaps require fuller records for definitive reconciliation.

brief.title: Predicting policy effects in new populations
possible: Governments could use earlier experiments to predict what a policy would cause in a new population before seeing results there. The prediction would include a useful range of uncertainty and state which relationships must stay stable for it to apply.
why: Earlier experiments could help governments compare programs and decide where a local trial is essential. Knowing which differences between populations matter could also focus data collection and reduce unnecessary repetition of experiments.

sources.showed: Policy effects varied substantially across development evaluations. Government-run programs had smaller effects than those run by academics or nongovernmental organisations, even after accounting for sample size.
sources.quote: I show that treatment effect heterogeneity can be appreciably reduced by taking study characteristics into account.
sources.cited_for: Differences in how programs are delivered deserve separate testing.
sources.not_established: The association does not show that government implementation itself caused smaller effects.

sources.showed: A working paper on public and private schooling found that, under stated assumptions, outside experimental estimates could predict local effects worse than biased local estimates.
sources.quote: In the data about private and public schools, under plausible assumptions, an exclusive reliance on the rigorous evidence has RMSE three times worse than using the biased OLS result from each context.
sources.cited_for: Reliable results from elsewhere can still produce poor local predictions.
sources.not_established: This schooling example does not establish that local observational estimates generally outperform predictions based on outside experiments.

sources.who: Fabian Manke-Reimers, Vincent Brugger, Till Bärnighausen and Stefan Kohler
sources.showed: Their review covered 64 studies transferring effect estimates between populations. Among applications lacking complete target data, none compared predictions with an effect estimate from the target population.
sources.quote:
How transportability methods were applied 
varied widely between studies, for instance in the covariate selection approach and sensitivity analysis.
sources.cited_for: Methods have practical applications, but direct testing in the target population remains important.
sources.not_established: The review does not establish dependable advance prediction for economic policies or rule out successes elsewhere.

sources.who: Xinran Miao, Jiwei Zhao and Hyunseung Kang
sources.showed: Their preprint calculated how assumptions about population differences changed predicted advertising effects in Georgia counties. No county remained sensitive after a correction for testing many counties.
sources.quote:
Our findings indicate that small departures from transportability can
lead to dramatically different ad effects across counties of Georgia.
sources.cited_for: Predictions can depend strongly on assumptions about unmeasured population differences.
sources.not_established: These calculations do not show observed trial reversals or establish a reliable way to detect false assumptions.

shown: Judea Pearl and Elias Bareinboim developed mathematical rules for when experimental results can identify effects in another population, given stated assumptions. Researchers have applied transfer methods and examined how predictions change when assumptions change. Dependable advance prediction across economic-policy populations remains an unresolved capability.
missing: Predictions fixed before new trial results need to succeed across meaningfully different policy populations.
Useful uncertainty ranges need to account for mistaken assumptions as well as limited samples.
Warnings need to identify consequential prediction failures without rejecting nearly every difficult case.
Independent teams need to reproduce results and repeat successful predictions in new settings at practical cost.

milestones.label: Predictions published before target results
milestones.explanation: Predictions, uncertainty ranges, applicability limits and evaluation rules would have to be registered and published before target results are seen. This would test advance prediction.

milestones.label: Population, delivery and scale tested separately
milestones.explanation: A prespecified trial suite would have to test population differences, delivery arrangements, scale changes and later-discovered influential differences separately. This would establish where transfer succeeds.

milestones.label: Useful uncertainty ranges prove reliable
milestones.explanation: Predicted ranges would have to capture effects reliably, account for noise in target trials and beat prespecified comparisons without becoming too broad. This would establish useful predictive accuracy.

milestones.label: Warnings earn their own assessment
milestones.explanation: Warnings and decisions to withhold predictions would have to identify consequential failures while preserving useful prediction coverage. This would test whether applicability limits help.

milestones.label: Independent teams repeat success on new populations
milestones.explanation: Independent teams would have to reproduce results and predict effects in new populations, with costs and practical limits documented. This would establish repeatability and tested breadth.

uncertain: How often do unmeasured population differences change policy effects enough to undermine predictions?
How diverse must the target trials be, and how narrow must uncertainty ranges become, to support policy decisions?
Can a method reliably recognise when its assumptions fail using information available before target results?

page.title: Prospective transport of economic policy effects
page.definition: A method uses earlier experiments and measured characteristics of a new population to predict a policy’s causal effect before that population’s outcomes are observed. Its predictions and uncertainty are tested against subsequent randomized experiments in the target population.

goal.need: Transport methods aim to reuse experiments when repeating them requires additional infrastructure, money and time. A review searched through 18 December 2024 found no comparison with a target effect estimate among applications lacking complete target treatment and outcome data. Its inclusion scope spans disciplines and does not establish the frequency of this gap in economic policy.

statements.quote: Making good policy decisions often comes down to being able to reasonably predict the effects of policy alternatives, and choosing those that maximize societal benefits.

completion.title: Independent prospective evaluation reproduces gains in predicting economic policy effects.
completion.criterion: An independent team repeats a prospective evaluation in a declared economic-policy domain. Predictions and a source-only benchmark are frozen before target outcomes. Across target randomized experiments, transported predictions have lower mean squared error, corrected for target-estimate sampling variance, and lower mean interval score than the benchmark. Interval scores concern predictive intervals for the trial estimates, including target sampling error, at the same prespecified nominal coverage. Target selection, outcomes, aggregation and benchmark are preregistered. Success establishes performance within the tested domain.
completion.set_by: Atlas fallback; no outside body’s combined completion criterion was found.
completion.basis: Searches of J-PAL, BITSS/SSPP, National Research Council guidance and policy-transportability research found no common numerical completion threshold. This Atlas proposal combines advance prediction, comparison with source-only evidence, uncertainty scoring and independent repetition. The cited sources support those components; none endorses this combined pass test. Interval scoring penalizes both interval width and observations outside the interval.

milestones.title: A proved transport formula identifies a target causal effect under stated assumptions.
milestones.criterion: For a specified selection diagram—a causal graph marking mechanisms that may differ between populations—derive the target intervention distribution from source experiments and target observations using do-calculus, the rules for transforming causal probability expressions. Selection variables must occur only as conditioning variables in terms without intervention operators. Pearl and Bareinboim’s 2014 Theorem 1 establishes this criterion conditional on the diagram; it does not empirically validate the diagram.
milestones.set_by: Pearl and Bareinboim, Statistical Science, Theorem 1; a mathematical identification criterion in transportability theory.
milestones.threshold_quote: is reducible, using the rules of do-calculus, to an expression in which $S$ appears only as a conditioning variable in do-free terms.

milestones.title: Randomized site effects benchmark predictions made using evidence from other sites.
milestones.criterion: Predict a site’s treatment effect using other sites and compare it with that site’s randomized treatment-effect estimate. Aggregate errors using root mean squared prediction error. Olsen et al.’s 2023 author summary reports accurate predictions in two randomized trials with little cross-site effect variation, involving gang prevention and student mentoring, and inaccurate predictions in trials with substantial variation. This published validation procedure supplies a retrospective test, without a universal accuracy cutoff.
milestones.set_by: Out-of-sample experimental benchmarking, as operationalized by Olsen et al. for education and youth interventions; the cited document is the authors’ summary.
milestones.threshold_quote: The prediction error for each site was estimated by taking the difference between the predicted impact and its impact estimate from the RCT.

milestones.title: Prospective transport predictions beat a source-only benchmark on effect error and interval score.
milestones.criterion: In a preregistered target-experiment set, predictions fixed before outcomes beat the source-only benchmark on both error and interval score, using the completion test’s treatment of sampling uncertainty. Independent repetition remains the completion test. Adjacent evidence: a working paper dated 9 April 2026 matches forecasts with results for 66 of 100 SSPP projects; it does not establish this source-to-target transport test. That working-paper result is not peer reviewed.
milestones.set_by: Atlas fallback; no published prospective economic-policy transport protocol setting this combined success threshold was found.

not_found: No outside criterion specifying a minimum number of target populations or an acceptable prospective policy-effect prediction error was found.
No independent prospective replication satisfying the proposed completion test was verified; this does not establish that none exists.
The Olsen article’s full text was inaccessible through the publisher and PMC; the cited evidence is its authors’ accessible summary.
